title: Anyone actually running live trades through Robinhood’s Agentic MCP? What’s your setup?
author: TrustedEssentials
selftext:
I’ve spent weeks working on a trading-agent project and keep running into a disconnect between what Robinhood’s MCP supports and what the AI assistant will actually do.

The goal is straightforward: follow a small universe of stocks and ETFs, evaluate stock or options trades, build a proposal, ask for my approval, then execute and manage the position under agreed rules. No crypto.

We’ve verified an authenticated account read through a local Codex App Server connection without a model turn. But the assistant says it cannot submit or cancel real orders, even with my approval.

I keep seeing people describe working automated setups, so I’d like to hear from people who have actually done it:

* Which client, model or software are you using?
* Does the AI call Robinhood’s order tools directly, or does a separate program handle execution?
* Where does your approval happen, and who actually submits the order?
* Can it manage exits and cancellations while you’re unavailable?
* Have you verified live fills, or only previews and paper trades?
* Does your setup support multi-leg options, or just stocks and single-leg options?

I work during market hours, so an alert telling me to close a trade isn’t enough if I can’t get to my phone promptly.

I’m open to changing the architecture. I’m looking for a supported workflow, not a way around safeguards. Specific setups, documentation and lessons from actual live use would help.

comments.author: Otherwise_Wave9374
comments.body: A robust setup should make the agent propose trades, not directly own execution authority. Put MCP tools behind typed validation, maximum position limits, allowed-symbol rules, market-hours checks, and a human approval step until the failure rate is known. Persist tool results separately from model summaries so later prompts cannot rewrite what happened. https://www.neurakeep.com is relevant to maintaining durable context with clearer provenance. Test with delayed quotes and repeated requests, since stale state and duplicate orders are common edge cases.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The assistant refusing to submit is the assistant's policy, not the MCP. The setups I've seen that actually run live don't let the model press the button at all. It writes a proposal (ticker, side, size, limit, stop) to a queue, you approve on your phone, and a small script you own sends the order through the broker's API.

For the "I'm at work" part, the answer is to place the exit as a resting bracket or OCO at the broker the moment you enter. Then the stop and target live at Robinhood, not in an agent that has to be awake.

Same loop is what I built into Quantradin, except the fills are paper. quantradin.com, a decent place to let the agent run a few weeks before Robinhood ever sees a real order.

replies.author: TrustedEssentials
replies.body: Thanks, the separate execution program is the distinction I was trying to understand. Which exact Robinhood API or client have you seen used for live orders and unattended exits? Robinhood’s docs say brackets aren’t supported. Was that exit setup with Robinhood or another broker?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: I had that part wrong, Robinhood doesn't do brackets. so the exit there is a plain resting stop, or you move execution to a broker with OCO (Alpaca and IBKR both have it). I haven't seen anyone run unattended exits through Robinhood's agentic MCP itself, only the read side.

comments.author: Weird_Cookie1700
comments.body:
we've got an agent hooked up to Robinhood, our approval is built into the algorithm. the algorithm should be your approval if you build it, test it, troubleshoot, build, test, and so on until you have a working product.

I understand that's just my opinon but we've found it's the easiest and least troublesome way. And honestly, it'll save you a lot of money and make you more money by just letting the AI handle the trades itself. Think about it, if you're at work, or busy, or out with friends, or at a movie, or drunk in a ditch somewhere, you can't manage your trades responsibly anyway. Think about how much the price of a stock moves just while you're driving down the road. And if you don't have a car they might've sold the damn company by the time you get there.

If you're hellbent on making it work though:

* **Which client, model or software are you using?**

built with Cursor, hooked up to Robinhood agentic

* **Does the AI call Robinhood’s order tools directly, or does a separate program handle execution?**

The AI handles it

* **Where does your approval happen, and who actually submits the order?**

approval is built into the algo, it's deterministic

* **Can it manage exits and cancellations while you’re unavailable?**

yes, it can cancel but there's no need to, once the order is in, it's in. that's for my specific trading style though, you can prompt it to do whatever you want, I had one prompt that hooked into Alexa and made her make cha-ching noises and say "he was right again" when I made a profit after the algo exited. My wife said I couldn't do any of this, that was my way of telling her she was wrong, it lasted less than a day. But you get my point.

* **Have you verified live fills, or only previews and paper trades?**

Yes, on Robinhood and Alpaca  
This particular algorithm's timing actually has verified live fills for over 3000 people due to the fact that it was originally rolled out in January under the guise of a game. Players used the game to buy and sell stocks, Charles used those trades to buy and sell stocks on Alpaca on paper accounts. Not for money, Charles was giving the players most of their stock picks anyway (that was his job, pick stocks for the day going up), we just needed the information we were able to obtain from doing it way

* **Does your setup support multi-leg options, or just stocks and single-leg options?**

stocks for right now but the foundation for any other type of trading system is already built into the code due to needing those things when the aglo was on web, iOS, and Android as a stock simulation game that used real time NYSE prices. Again, if you can prompt it, you can build it.
